synopsis: Harmonized standards are officially listed under European law and give a presumption of conformity only within their scope; EN 474 offers such a route where cited, but is not an automatic-braking performance matrix [f15075, f15080, f2719]. In 2026, the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 list was still being prepared, no standards had yet been cited according to the skeptic’s review, and future harmonization of EN 474 or EN ISO 21815 remained unverified, so a status checkpoint is recommended immediately before the 2027 declaration [f2208, f10501, f11217, f2209, f15084]. FprEN ISO 19014-1 was linked to the Regulation through M/605, adopted on 20 January 2025, with publication planned for 22 November 2026; this does not establish that it had been cited, while the possible interim use of AI Act standards until delegated acts expected by 2 August 2028 remained unverified commentary [f10538, f11218, f11219, f7431]. Great Britain designated the EN 474:2022 family on 8 August 2026 under its separate machinery regime, providing a presumption-of-conformity route and a parallel declaration calendar, although the claimed notice number 0139/26 was not confirmed [f15244, f15496, f2875]. Where no harmonized standard fits automatic braking, the manufacturer’s own safety case must demonstrate safety using the state of the art, with standards providing evidence even when not harmonized and a lawyer expecting comparison against Volvo, Caterpillar and Komatsu systems [f15082, f15085, f11133]. Standards are generally voluntary but acquire legal significance through legislation, harmonization or designation, contracts, procurement requirements, or the manufacturer’s chosen state-of-the-art route [f2144, f15083].
